[THOUGHT] The key immediate data to distinguish physiologic neonatal jaundice from hemolysis or conjugated causes is the bilirubin level and fraction (total and direct). This single test will guide urgency (phototherapy/ET) and narrow differential. I will request serum total and direct bilirubin.

[TEST] Order: Serum total bilirubin and direct (conjugated) bilirubin levels.

[THOUGHT] A 5-day-old with total bilirubin 7 mg/dL and direct 0.6 mg/dL has mild, predominantly unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia occurring at the typical age for physiologic neonatal jaundice. Values are below usual treatment thresholds and there is no significant direct (conjugated) fraction to suggest cholestasis. In the absence of additional concerning features (severe anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, dark urine, poor feeding/dehydration, or a positive Coombs), the most likely diagnosis is the normal physiologic jaundice of the newborn due to transient immaturity of bilirubin conjugation.

[DIAGNOSIS] Physiologic (unconjugated) neonatal jaundice.
